title: Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60)
html:
Abhidhamma · Chapter 3

Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60)

Pages 41–60 (20 pages)
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 41

Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this process. We cannot determine where we will be born next. We cannot arrange things so that at our death the right things will occur to us and we will obtain a happy rebirth. Whatever persons surround us or help us they cannot determine our last thought process. It depends upon deeds in the past what happens to us at death.” And not only at death: “It is further deeds that determine our body, the family we are born into, whether we will be wealthy or not, whether we will die at an early age; everything that we experience29 is because of deeds in the past.”

The book says: “You can see then how important an understanding of moral and immoral deeds is. Without this understanding beings wander through life sometimes doing the most atrocious30 things to each other. All of this happens through ignorance of the true nature of the law of cause and effect.” The only thing that can be done about the last moment of this life is done now, by the kind of citta (consciousness) that arises31 in this moment.

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. process: a row of moments that follow one another in order 16. hinder: to get in the way of; to hold back 2. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly 17. craving: strong wanting; a thirst for something being 18. bough: a big branch of a tree 3. morality: good conduct; not killing, not stealing, not lying 19. nay: no and the rest 20. ere: before 4. immoral: bad conduct; wrong 21. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a 5. deed: something done; an act, good or bad sound, a thought 6. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really 22. habitual: done out of habit, again and again there 23. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, 7. enumerate: to count up and list one by one kindness, patience, understanding 8. plane: a world or level where beings live: the human world, 24. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not the heavens, the animal world and so on knowing 9. woeful: full of sorrow; very unhappy 25. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; 10. titan: a kind of being that loves fighting anger, even a little 11. matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel 26. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, anything, such as hardness, colour or sound such as seeing or hearing 12. rebirth: being born again in a new life after this one ends 27. conception: the very start of a new life inside the mother 13. realm: a kingdom; here, one of the worlds that beings can 28. womb: the place inside a mother where a baby grows be born in 29. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the 14. suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give knowing itself lasting happiness 30. atrocious: very cruel and terrible 15. discourse: a talk or sermon; here, one of the Buddha's talks 31. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen written down

Lesson 8: the four stages of enlightenment

“Streamwinner (sotapanna) means one has entered the stream to final enlightenment”

A way out. The wheel has no beginning, but it has an end for the one who understands. “The process1 by which one comes to understand the truth is also explained in the Abhidhamma. There are four stages of enlightenment2.” The book names them: “first the stream-winner, second the once-returner, third the neverreturner and fourth the fully-enlightened one”. In Pāḷi: sotāpanna (stream-enterer), sakadāgāmī (oncereturner), anāgāmī (never-returner) and arahant (fully enlightened).

The ten fetters. What holds a being3 to the wheel is called a saṃyojana (fetter4), a chain. There are ten, and the four stages are four cuttings of the chain.

rule and attachment to wrong view aversion restlessness ritual formless

attachment to doubt sense desire conceit ignorance form

cut at the first stage cut at the third (worn thin at the second) cut at the fourth stage sotāpanna · sakadāgāmī · anāgāmī · arahant “There are then, ten fetters which bind us to the wheel of existence.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  42

Page 42
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 43

Fetter Pāḷi Cut at sakkāya diṭṭhi (personality first stage wrong view5 belief) doubt vicikicchā first stage adherence to rule and ritual sīlabbata parāmāsa first stage sense desire kāma rāga third stage (weakened at the second) vyāpāda third stage (weakened at the aversion6 second) rūpa rāga fourth stage attachment7 to existence in the form realms8 attachment to existence in the arūpa rāga fourth stage formless realms māna fourth stage conceit9 uddhacca fourth stage restlessness10 avijjā fourth stage ignorance11

The first stage. “At the first stage, a being has eliminated12 the first three fetters which bind one to the wheel of existence.” Wrong view is “an incorrect view of the way things are, i.e., that there is a self, that there really are permanent people and things rather than just momentary13 physical and mental14 phenomena15“. Doubt is doubt “about the truth of the Dhamma”. Adherence to rule and ritual is the belief “that there is a method or a technique or something which one performs that will lead one to enlightenment”. The sotāpanna (stream-enterer) has seen for himself that there is only nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter16), so the belief in a self cannot come back, and he cannot believe that any ceremony could have done it for him.

“Streamwinner (sotapanna) means one has entered the stream to final enlightenment and that there are no more conditions17 to be born in a lower plane18 than that of a human being.” The stream-enterer still has attachment and anger. He can still be born again, but never in the four unhappy planes, and the ancient texts say he will reach the end within seven lives at most.

The dirt on a fingernail. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya (the Grouped Discourses19) the Buddha once picked up a little dirt on his fingernail and asked the monks20: “Which is more: the little bit of dirt on my fingernail, or this great earth?” They answered: “Sir, the great earth is far more. The little bit of dirt on your fingernail is tiny.” In the same way, he said, for the sotāpanna (stream-enterer) the suffering21 that is finished is like the great earth, and the suffering that remains, in seven lives at the most, is like the dirt on the fingernail: “what’s left is tiny.”

The second stage. “A once-returner (sakadagami) lessens his attachment and aversion. He is called oncereturner because he can return only once more to the human plane.” The next two fetters are not yet cut, only worn thin.

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  43

Page 43
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 44

The third stage. “A never-returner (anagami) eliminates two further fetters, these being sense-desire and aversion. He has no more desire for sense-objects22 and no more dislike for unpleasant things. The neverreturner does not return to the human plane again. If he dies as an anagami he is born into a god realm where he attains final enlightenment.” Those realms are the five highest Brahmā (highest heavenly) planes of fine matter, which the ancient texts call the Suddhāvāsa (the Pure Abodes), because only never-returners are born there.

The fourth stage. “The last stage is the fully enlightened one (the arahant). He has eliminated the last five fetters which bind him to the wheel of existence. They are attachment to existence in the form-god realms, attachment to existence in the formless-god realms, conceit, restlessness and ignorance. Because of the first of these two fetters beings are born into the god realms. When they are eliminated there is no more desire for any existence at all.” “There are then, ten fetters which bind us to the wheel of existence.”

Moments, not people. Each stage is reached at one moment of lokuttara citta (consciousness23 beyond the world), the magga citta (path consciousness), which experiences24 nibbāna (the end of all troubles) and cuts the fetters for good. It is followed at once by phala citta (fruition25 consciousness), which also experiences nibbāna (the end of all troubles). Lesson 3 counted these among the eighty-nine. After the fourth path moment there is no more kusala (good) and no more akusala (bad), because there is no more kamma (deed26) to make. Everything the arahant (fully enlightened one) does from then on is kiriya (functional27).

What happens when an arahant dies? The book asks and answers. “He has eliminated all unwholesome28 tendencies29 from his character including the desire to go on being born. Having become enlightened during this life, he will die at the time when his lifespan30 has expired31. Since there is no more desire to go on, when the last moment of life for the arahant finishes it is not followed by another rebirth32 consciousness. When we die, it is immediately followed by another moment (of the next life); when an arahant dies, that is all. No more experience. No more rebirth. This is called by the Buddha the only true peace.”

Not a ladder either. Nobody climbs the four stages by wanting to. The fetters are cut by paññā (wisdom) that has seen nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) as they are, moment after moment, for a long time. Reading a list of ten fetters cuts none of them. But the first of them, the view that there is a self, is the one that every lesson in this course has been about.

The answers are at the back.

Lesson 9: the chain, the four truths and the three marks

“Koṇḍañña has really understood! Koṇḍañña has really understood!”

The book says: “There are three more aspects which should be discussed—the Law of Dependent Origination1, the three basic characteristics2 of existence and the Four Noble Truths.”

Dependent origination. Paṭicca samuppāda (dependent origination) “is the Buddha’s explanation of how states of existence come to be and how they condition3 each other”. The book sets it out as a chain of links:

avijjā ignorance jarā-maraṇa saṅkhāra decay and death deeds 1 12 2 jāti viññāṇa birth consciousness

round bhava nāma-rūpa and round becoming mind and matter

upādāna saḷāyatana grasping six bases

taṇhā phassa craving contact vedanā feeling “We can see then that at the root of it all is ignorance.”

1. Dependent on avijjā (ignorance4) arise5 saṅkhāra (karmic activities, deeds6)

2. Dependent on saṅkhāra (deeds) arises viññāṇa (consciousness7)

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  47

Page 47
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 48

3. Dependent on viññāṇa (consciousness) arise nāma-rūpa (mind and matter8) 4. Dependent on nāma-rūpa (mind and matter) arise saḷāyatana (the six-fold bases, the five senses and thinking) 5. Dependent on saḷāyatana (the six bases) arises phassa (contact) 6. Dependent on phassa (contact) arises vedanā (feeling) 7. Dependent on vedanā (feeling) arises taṇhā (craving9) 8. Dependent on taṇhā (craving) arises upādāna (grasping10) 9. Dependent on upādāna (grasping) arises bhava (becoming) 10. Dependent on bhava (becoming) arises jāti (birth) 11. Dependent on jāti (birth) arise jarā-maraṇa (decay and death), sorrow, lamentation11, pain, grief12 and despair13 “Thus arises the whole mass of suffering14.” The links are turning all the time. Because of ignorance, deeds are done; because of deeds, a new life begins; with it come mind and matter, the senses, contact, feeling, wanting, grasping, a new existence, birth, old age and death. And then round again.

Seen the other way, the chain is a way out: when ignorance ends, the deeds that make rebirth15 are not done, and the rest does not arise. “We can see then that at the root of it all is ignorance. That is defined as ignorance of the Four Noble Truths.”

The Four Noble Truths. The Buddha taught them first, in the deer park at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī (Benares), to the five ascetics16 who had once been his companions. In Pāḷi the four are dukkha (suffering), samudaya (its origin), nirodha (its ending) and magga (the path):

1. Life is unsatisfactory17 or suffering: dukkha (suffering). 2. Suffering arises because of craving: taṇhā (craving). 3. There is an ending of suffering, which is nibbāna (the end of all troubles), the stopping of craving. 4. The way leading to the ending of suffering is the ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga (the Noble Eightfold Path).

The first sermon. The discourse18 in which the Buddha taught these truths is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (the Discourse on Setting the Wheel of the Teaching in Motion). Two months after his enlightenment19 he walked to Isipatana, where the five ascetics were staying. They had left him when he gave up starving himself, and they agreed not to rise for him. But as he came near they could not keep to it: one took his bowl, one made a seat, one brought water for his feet. He told them that there are two extremes that should not be followed: indulgence20 in sensual21 pleasures, and tormenting22 oneself. Between them lies the middle way, the Eightfold Path. Then he taught the Four Noble Truths. As he spoke, the eldest of the five, Koṇḍañña, saw the truth for himself: “Everything that is liable23 to arise is liable to cease24.” The Buddha said: “Koṇḍañña has really understood! Koṇḍañña has really understood!” Koṇḍañña had become a sotāpanna (stream-enterer), the first of the Buddha’s disciples25 to do so.

“When one does not understand these truths directly one is subject to continual rebirth in the wheel of existence.” The eight factors of the path are: right understanding, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood26, right effort, right mindfulness27 and right concentration28.

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  48

Page 48

The path is made of moments. The Eightfold Path “is often taught as a ‘path’ which one follows by developing each of the factors piece by piece until there are all perfected. In the Abhidhamma it is made clear that the Eightfold Path is in fact only momentary29 phenomena30 like everything else. The Eightfold Path is not a ‘whole path’ which one follows, but at the moment that a wholesome31 moment of wisdom (the wisdom that understands the true nature of things) arises then it is accompanied by the Eightfold Path factors as mental factors32 (cetasikas).” The eight factors are eight cetasika (mental33 factors) from Lesson 4. Right understanding is paññā (wisdom). Right thought is vitakka (applied thought). Right effort is viriya (effort). Right mindfulness is sati (mindfulness). Right concentration is ekaggatā (concentration). Right speech, right action and right livelihood are the three virati (abstinences34).

the eight factors are eight cetasika (mental factors)

right understanding right thought right effort right mindfulness paññā vitakka viriya sati

right concentration right speech right action right livelihood ekaggatā virati virati virati

five arise together at every moment of true wisdom three arise one at a time, when there is something to abstain fro all eight arise together only at the moment of enlightenment “Five of these factors accompany every moment of true wisdom. The whole eight occur together only at the moments of enlightenment.”

“Five of these factors accompany every moment of true wisdom. The whole eight occur together only at the moments of enlightenment.” The five are understanding, thought, effort, mindfulness and concentration. The three abstinences arise one at a time, when there is something to abstain from. Only at the moment of magga citta (path consciousness), when nibbāna (the end of all troubles) is experienced35, do all eight arise at once. So nobody walks the path. The path arises for one moment, falls away36, and arises again when the conditions are there.

The three marks. “Finally, the Buddha also explained that there are three things characterising all elements37 of existence.” Every citta (consciousness), every cetasika (mental factor) and every rūpa (matter) has these three marks:

dukkha (unsatisfactory): “there is no lasting satisfaction in them” anicca (impermanent38): “they do not last even for a moment” anattā (non-self39): “there is not a lasting person, self or something in anything, they are all empty of self”

What does not last cannot give lasting satisfaction, and what does not last and cannot satisfy cannot be anyone’s self. The ancient texts call these the tilakkhaṇa (the three characteristics). The chariot40, the moments, the eighty-nine, the fifty-two, the twenty-eight, the seed and the fruit, the wheel and the fetters41 all point at the same three facts.

One root. Ignorance begins the chain; wisdom ends it. The next lesson asks where that wisdom has to begin.

Lesson 10: what is happening right now?

“When we sit down how do we know that we are sitting?”

The point of the lists. The book ends by asking the question any reader will have been asking. “You may wonder what is the point of all these classifications1. Are they of any use to one in coming to understanding the truth of the way things are?” Its answer: “When the Abhidhamma enumerates2 lists of types of consciousness3 and lists of types of matter4 this is so that one can understand that this is all that there really is right now.” Right now, in this moment, there is nothing but some of the eighty-nine, some of the fifty-two and some of the twenty-eight.

Sitting. The book takes the plainest thing it can find. “We sit and we talk and we think and we move about but we do not realise that our sitting and talking and thinking, etc., are in fact conditioned5 by many different things. When we sit down how do we know that we are sitting? You may say, ‘Well it’s obvious, isn’t it?’ But ‘sitting’ is known because of different experiences6 through the body-sense7 and the eye perhaps, and we remember that these experiences when occurring all together are conventionally8 known as sitting.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  51

Page 51
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 52

hardness knows nothing rūpa (matter) body-sense consciousness experiences the hardness take it apart nāma (mind) “sitting” one word seeing sees colour, at another moment nāma (mind) saññā (memory) remembers “this is sitting” nāma (mind) four realities, at four different moments, and no person in any of them “So in reality no ‘person’ exists who is ‘sitting’ on a ‘chair’.”

“It is, in fact, a type of (body-sense) consciousness which experiences hardness through the body, seeing which sees and memory which remembers what we are doing. Body-sense, seeing and memory are all types of nama which are conditioned. They are each different and each have different functions9. Hardness is a type of rupa (matter). It cannot know anything about anything. Hardness is not a seat. ‘Seat’ or ‘chair’ are conventional labels we give to other sets of experience through different senses. None of these experiences is a person sitting. Each is different. Each experience occurs at a different moment. So in reality10 no ‘person’ exists who is ‘sitting’ on a ‘chair’. There are just different realities occurring one after another through different senses.”

So, in the moment that is called “sitting”, there is:

hardness, which is rūpa (matter) and knows nothing; the body-sense citta (consciousness) that experiences the hardness, which is nāma (mind); seeing, which sees colour, another nāma (mind) at another moment; saññā (memory), the cetasika (mental factor11) that remembers “this is sitting”, at yet another moment.

Four different realities, at different moments. The word “sitting” is the box they are put in. The word “I” is the box the box is put in.

Pain. “This may still not seem clear, but perhaps if we apply this knowledge to all of our life, we can see that pain, for example, is just unpleasant result12 (of deeds13 in the past), that the aversion14 to pain is just nama, that the unpleasant feeling when there is pain is also just nama.” When a child falls and scrapes a knee, the sting is vipāka (result), and cannot be helped; the “I hate this” that follows is not result, and can be known as dosa (anger), arising15 and falling away16.

Insults. “When people insult us, it is just sound appearing through the ear.” Hearing the sound is vipāka (result). The sound is rūpa (matter); it knows nothing. The meaning is put together afterwards by thinking, and the hurt is dosa (anger) arising in a later moment. “It is only when we see and hear ‘things’ which we don’t like that we have all our problems, worries, strife17 and woe18.”

No person in them. The book’s last teaching sentence: “To understand Abhidhamma is to understand that there is just seeing, hearing, thinking, touching, tasting, etc., but no person in them. This knowledge as it develops, ultimately19 brings us release20 from this unsatisfactory21 wheel of existence.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  52

Page 52
Abhidhamma Nobody is in charge. “We have no control over this (p. 41–60) p. 53

Every lesson has been about this sentence. Lesson 2 said that seeing is nāma (mind) and colour is rūpa (matter). Lesson 3 said that seeing is a vipāka citta (result consciousness), one of eighty-nine. Lesson 4 said that it arises with seven cetasika (mental22 factors). Lesson 5 said that the eye-sense and the colour are among the twenty-eight kinds of rūpa (matter). Lesson 6 said that the seeing is the fruit of a deed. Lesson 7 said that this body and this life are the fruit of deeds too. Lesson 8 said that the view of a self in all this is the first fetter23 to be cut. Lesson 9 said that seeing is anicca (impermanent24), dukkha (unsatisfactory) and anattā (non-self25).

What the Abhidhamma is for. The preface to the book says: “A study of the Abhidhamma can be of immense value to us in coming to terms with the nature of life and understanding it in the way of momentary26 events.” And: “As we understand more and more the Buddha’s teaching, we will be more kind, more considerate27 and more harmless (in the true sense of causing no harm) to all our fellow beings28.”

The last word. The book closes with a verse from the Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity29) by Buddhaghosa, which it calls “the greatest written summary of the Theravadin teachings in existence today”:

As long as a man is vague30 about the world, About its origin31, about its ceasing32, About the means that lead to its cessation, So long he cannot recognise the truths.

The world is this moment of nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter). Its origin is craving33 and ignorance34. Its ceasing is nibbāna (the end of all troubles). The means is the path, arising moment by moment.

Lesson 11: no one is master

“Greed, hate, and delusion:—these three make for trouble, for suffering, for distress.”

The second essay in the book is by Nina van Gorkom, and it is called Abhidhamma and Practice. The first essay explained what the Abhidhamma says. The second asks what difference it makes.

Three things. The essay opens with a question: “What is the cause of all misery and sorrow in the world?” It answers with a discourse1 from the Saṃyutta Nikāya (the Grouped Discourses, called the Kindred Sayings in the translation it uses), in which King Pasenadi of Kosala asked the Buddha:

“How many kinds of things, lord, that happen in the world, make for trouble, for suffering2, for distress?”

The Buddha answered:

“Three things, sire, happen of that nature. What are the three? Greed, hate, and delusion3:—these three make for trouble, for suffering, for distress.”

Greed is lobha (attachment4); hate is dosa (anger); delusion is moha (ignorance5): the three roots of Lesson 3. “In the Buddha’s time defilements6 were the cause of all sorrow and suffering and this is also true for today. It is true for all times. Only those who are perfected have no more sorrow and suffering.”

The solution. “The Buddha taught the solution to all problems: the eradication7 of all unwholesomeness8 through the development of right understanding; right understanding of all phenomena9 of our life.” Is it selfish to be busy with one’s own defilements? And is it even possible? “We cannot eradicate the defilements of others, ‘we’ cannot even eradicate our own defilements. But when right understanding has been developed, it is right understanding which can gradually eradicate defilements. But this may take many lives.” Nobody does it; paññā (wisdom) does it. And as for selfishness: “We usually seek only

Realities and concepts. Things like “person, animal, tree or house are not paramattha dhammas, they are concepts.” A paññatti (concept) is an idea put together by thinking: “We form up concepts because of a combination of many different experiences which we remember.” Colour is a reality33; “tree” is a concept. Hardness is a reality; “chair” is a concept. The realities “can be directly experienced by everybody, without there being the need to think about them. We do not have to think of sound or hardness in order to experience them.” Concepts can only be thought. This does not mean that thinking is wrong: “We should not try to avoid thinking of people or things, thinking is a reality, it arises. However, we should know that the concepts which are objects of our thinking are not realities.”

Blame. “When there is no right understanding of nama and rupa we will only have a superficial34 knowledge of both ourselves and others. We will have a wrong understanding of cause and effect in life. Don’t we blame others for our own unhappiness? The real cause of unhappiness is within ourselves.” When a boy is unhappy because his sister took the last mango, the mango and the sister are not the cause. The cause is lobha (attachment) and dosa (anger), which arose in him, and which will arise again at the next mango unless paññā (wisdom) comes to know them. “Right understanding of the different namas and rupas which appear is the only way to have less defilements and thus to have less sorrow in life.”

Lesson 12: study with mindfulness

“What appears through the body-sense? Not a person, not my husband.”

What the practice is. The second half of Nina van Gorkom’s essay is about vipassanā (insight1): “The development of insight is a kind of study of nama and rupa through the direct experience2 of them.” Not study in a book, though the book comes first, but study at the moment a reality3 appears. “Namas and rupas which appear one at a time should be ‘studied’ with mindfulness4, but each moment of study is extremely short, since mindfulness does not last, it falls away5. However, gradually a clearer understanding of realities can be accumulated6.” The objects7 of this study are “nama and rupa”, “not people, animals or things”. “Wherever we are there are in reality only nama and rupa, such as seeing, hearing, the visible object, sound or hardness.”

What mindfulness is. Sati (mindfulness) is one of the nineteen beautiful mental factors8 in Lesson 4. “Mindfulness (sati) is nama which arises9 with a wholesome10 moment of consciousness11. We cannot induce mindfulness whenever we want it, but it can arise when there are the appropriate conditions12. All namas and rupas in our life arise only when there are the appropriate conditions, not because of our will.” So there is no method of making sati (mindfulness) happen. There is only the question of its conditions.
